definition: Palatial means resembling a palace in grand size and luxury.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word palatial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know palatial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The opera house lobby was palatial, all marble columns, gilded balconies, and chandeliers the size of rowboats.
A spacious room simply offers plenty of space, while a palatial one carries the sweeping grandeur and luxury of a palace.
A palatial mansion imitates the luxury of a palace, but a monumental structure is built on a scale so colossal that it dwarfs everything around it.

Grand means impressively large and splendid, and either half can dominate - a grand staircase, a grand gesture, a grand old courtroom. Palatial pins the comparison to one building in particular: the place resembles a palace, with all the sweeping size and luxury that implies. A courtroom can be grand on dignity alone; palatial requires square footage worthy of royalty.

Magnificent means strikingly beautiful and elaborate, and it fits any scale - a magnificent tapestry, a magnificent sunset, a magnificent hall. Palatial is specifically about built space that matches a palace in grand size and luxury. A pocket watch can be magnificent; only something you can wander through can be palatial.

Instead they found a palatial residence: a ballroom lined with gilded mirrors, a dining hall that seated forty, twin marble staircases, and grounds that took an hour to walk.

descriptive, journalistic register
Palatial describes physical grandeur only: buildings, rooms, estates, and lobbies that look and feel like palaces.
It does not describe a person's wealth or behavior, and it is not a synonym for expensive; a tiny diamond costs a fortune, but nothing about it is palatial.

When the Regal Theater opened in 1927, newspapers struggled to describe a building whose only business was showing films.
Its lobby rose four stories under a painted sky; ushers in braided uniforms led patrons up twin sweeping staircases wide enough for royal processions.
Critics called the place palatial, and the owners took it as a business plan rather than a compliment: for the price of a ticket, a factory worker spent an evening living like a king.
The auditorium seated three thousand beneath a ceiling of gilded plaster and hidden stars.
Historians of architecture note the irony — the age of democratic entertainment announced itself in the borrowed costume of monarchy.
